unit.title: Assemble & disassemble scaffolding to enable access to the work area

summary: This unit teaches you to plan safe access for welding work at height and, as part of a trained and authorised team, to put up, inspect, use and take down mobile towers and frame scaffolds. You will learn the parts of a scaffold, how to check them, how to build a level, braced and guarded platform following the maker's instructions, how inspection tags work, how to weld and cut safely from a scaffold, how Jamaica's weather and sites affect scaffolds, and how to lead a team through the work.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). Welders often work above the ground: brackets on columns, canopies on walls, pipe supports, tank roofs. The safest way to reach most of this work is a proper working platform: a **mobile tower** or a **scaffold**, built, inspected and taken down correctly.

Falls from height are among the most common causes of death and serious injury in construction and fabrication work. A scaffold fails when a step is skipped: a leg on soft ground, a missing brace, a guardrail left off "for a minute", a tower moved with someone on it, or a welding lead clamped to the frame.

blocks.note: Under the Centre's rules, only people who are **trained and authorised** may erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold or tower, and trainees do so only under the direct supervision of the Centre's trained scaffold instructor. This kit teaches the knowledge you need; it does not make you competent to build scaffolds alone.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Who it is for:** Level 3 welders and team leaders who plan access for welding at height and work as part of a supervised scaffold team.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Plan safe access
Choose between a ladder, tower, frame scaffold or mobile elevating work platform (MEWP); survey the site; write a short access plan.
Know the components
Name and recognise standards, ledgers, transoms, braces, couplers, base plates, base jacks, sole boards, boards, guardrails and toe boards.
Check components
Inspect every part before use; tag and quarantine faulty ones.
Erect towers and scaffolds
Follow the maker's instructions: firm base, level and square first lift, braces, boards, guardrails before standing on a level, safe ladder access.
Protect against falls
Full edge protection, boarded platforms, harnesses where the rules require, and a rescue plan.
Inspect and tag
Know when scaffolds are inspected, what is checked, and how tags show whether a scaffold may be used.
Weld and cut from a scaffold safely
Fire precautions, the return lead on the work, cylinders on the ground, no hot work on the scaffold itself.
Dismantle and store
Top down in reverse order, parts lowered never thrown, ties removed last, parts checked and racked.
Lead the team
Brief, give roles and signals, supervise each step and stop unsafe work.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning access, the Centre's rules, components, mobile towers, edge protection, platforms, ladders, erection, fall protection, ties, loads, inspection and tags, hot work, overhead hazards, exclusion zones, dismantling, storage, weather and leading the team.
A **written paper** with short answers (component names, the ladder angle, points of contact, tag, brake, lift, fire watch, tie, exclusion zone) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals**, under the scaffold instructor: plan, erect, inspect, tag and dismantle a mobile tower for a welding job; and erect a frame scaffold bay on uneven ground with ladder access, find planted faults, then dismantle and store it.

sections.title: Choosing safe access for work at height

blocks.p: Before choosing equipment, ask three questions in order: **Can the work be done without going up** (for example by fabricating the part on the ground and lifting it into place)? If not, **what equipment will stop a fall happening** (a guarded platform)? Only if that is not possible, **what will reduce the harm if someone falls** (a harness and a rescue plan)?

head: Access
Good for
Limits
rows: Ladder or stepladder
Short, light tasks: a quick look, a measurement, getting onto a platform
One hand needed to hold on, so not for welding, which needs both hands, a helmet and a steady stance
No edge protection
Mobile tower (aluminium)
Welding brackets on columns or pipe supports inside a shop; work at one spot for hours or days; can be moved when empty
Needs firm, level ground
Height limited by its base and outriggers, as the maker says
Must never be moved with anyone or anything on it
Frame or tube-and-fitting scaffold
Long runs of welding along a wall, canopy or tank; jobs lasting days or weeks; heavier loads
Takes longer to erect
Usually needs ties to the structure
Designed and inspected by competent people
Mobile elevating work platform (MEWP): scissor lift or boom lift
Work spread along a wall or high up, on firm level ground, for a short time at each spot
Trained operator only
Ground must carry it
Harness needed in boom lifts
Limited platform load

ul: **Height and extent** of the work, and how long it will take.
**Ground:** firm and level enough? Soft soil, fill, slopes, drains, manhole covers and suspended floors.
**Overhead hazards:** power lines, cranes, roof edges.
**Traffic and people:** forklifts, vehicles, public walkways, other trades working below.
**The structure:** can it take ties? Is the wall sound?
**Weather:** wind exposure, rain, sun, the season.

blocks.p: Write down, before erection starts: the type of scaffold or tower and the maker's instructions to be used; the platform height and size; the loads it must carry (people, tools, steel); the base (sole boards, base plates, base jacks, outriggers); ties; access (built-in ladder, stairs or a tied ladder); edge protection; the exclusion zone; the hot-work precautions; and who will erect, inspect and use it.

blocks.note: The choice of access is made in the plan, not on the morning of the job with whatever is lying in the yard. If the plan says a tower, the team does not swap to a ladder because the tower is "too much trouble" to build.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Type
What it is
rows: Mobile aluminium tower
Prefabricated frames, braces and platforms on castors, built to the maker's instructions
Frame scaffold
Steel frames (standards and ledgers welded together) joined with braces, base jacks and boards
Tube-and-fitting scaffold
Loose steel tubes (usually 48.3 mm outside diameter) joined by couplers; very flexible, but every joint depends on the right coupler, correctly tightened
System scaffold
Standards with fixed connection points (rosettes or cups) into which ledgers and braces lock

head: Part
What it is and what it does
rows: Standard
An upright tube that carries the load down to the ground
Ledger
A horizontal tube running along the length of the scaffold, joining the standards
Transom
A short horizontal tube across the width of the scaffold that carries the boards (a putlog is a transom with one end built into the wall)
Brace
A diagonal tube that stops the scaffold swaying or folding (facade braces along the face; ledger braces across the width)
Lift
The height from one level of ledgers to the next (often about 2 m)
Bay
The space between two pairs of standards along the scaffold
Base plate
A steel plate under each standard that spreads its load; the standard sits squarely in its centre
Base jack (adjustable base)
A screw jack under a standard to level the scaffold on uneven ground, used within the maker's maximum extension
Sole board
A timber board under base plates on soft or uneven ground, spreading the load so the leg cannot sink
Boards (platform)
Timber, steel or aluminium boards forming the working platform
Guardrail and mid rail
Horizontal rails along the open edges of a platform to stop people falling
Toe board
An upright board along the platform edge to stop tools and materials being kicked off
Tie
A fixing that holds the scaffold to the building or structure so it cannot pull away or topple
Castor
A wheel on a tower leg, with a brake that must be locked before anyone climbs
Outrigger (stabiliser)
An arm fixed to a tower's legs to widen its base and make it more stable

head: Fitting
Use
Point to know
rows: Right-angle (double) coupler
Joins two tubes at 90°, such as a ledger to a standard
A load-bearing coupler
Swivel coupler
Joins two tubes at any angle, such as a brace to a standard
Used for bracing
Putlog (single) coupler
Holds a transom or putlog onto a ledger
Not made to carry the load of a ledger on a standard: never use it in place of a right-angle coupler
Sleeve coupler
Joins two tubes end to end on the outside
Stronger in bending than a joint pin
Joint pin (spigot)
Joins two tubes end to end from the inside
Not for joints that will be pulled apart (in tension)
Base plate, base jack
Under standards
Standard central on the plate; jack within its limit

blocks.note: Each coupler is tightened with a scaffold spanner to the torque the standard or maker gives. A coupler that is too loose slips; one that is badly over-tightened can crack or strip its bolt.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: The ground must be firm and level enough for the base. Check for soft soil, fill, recent digging, slopes and water.
On soft or uneven ground, lay **sole boards** under the base plates to spread the load. A single sole board is often run under two standards.
Never stand a leg on a drain cover, manhole cover, loose bricks or blocks: they can break or slide. Move the leg, or bridge the cover as a competent person decides.

On a slope, use **base jacks** within the maker's maximum extension. If a jack would need winding out further, level the low side another way that the maker or a competent person approves, such as stepped sole boards or a different frame height. Never pack with loose bricks or offcuts.
Inside a building, check that a suspended floor can carry the scaffold and its load.
A tall or long scaffold against a building is **tied** to it so that it cannot pull away or topple. The design or the maker's instructions say where and how often.

Ties need sound anchorage. Old stone, loose blockwork, gutters, drainpipes and window frames are not anchors. If the wall is doubtful, a competent person tests the anchors, or the scaffold is held up another way, such as rakers or buttresses.
Sheeting, netting or banners fixed to a scaffold or tower catch the wind like a sail and greatly increase the load on the ties and base. They are fitted only when the design allows for them.

blocks.p: Each scaffold is built for a **duty**: light, general or heavy. The platform's rated load (for example about 150 kg per square metre for a light-duty platform, and 300 kg or more for a heavy one) is on the tag, the drawing or the maker's instructions. A platform must also never carry a heavy **point load**: a pile of steel in the middle of a board can break the board even when the total is within the rating. Keep stacks small, spread them out, and place them near the standards and transoms.

head: Component
Reject or tag it if you find
rows: Tubes and frames
Bends, dents, splits, cracked welds, heavy rust or pitting (especially at the ends), ends not square
Couplers
Cracks, bent or worn bolts, stripped or stiff threads, distorted jaws
Base plates and base jacks
Bent plates, bent or seized screws, missing nuts
Timber boards
Splits, rot, large knots, warping, burn marks, missing end bands
Metal boards and platforms
Dents, cracks, broken hooks or latches, damaged trapdoors
Ladders
Bent or missing rungs, damaged stiles, missing feet
Castors
Brakes that do not lock, damaged wheels, loose legs
Guardrails, toe boards and clips
Bends, cracks, missing or broken clips and locking pins

blocks.p: Any faulty part is **tagged or marked as faulty, set apart in a quarantine area and reported**, so it cannot be used by mistake. It is repaired only by a competent person, or scrapped. A welder must never weld a scaffold part to repair it.

blocks.note: Steel tubes and frames stored near the sea rust fast, from Kingston Harbour to the north coast. Rust that pits the wall of a tube makes it thinner and weaker, and the damage is often worst at the ends and inside. Set heavily rusted or pitted parts aside for a competent person to judge.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Every tower and frame scaffold system is different. The maker's instructions give the order of assembly, the bracing, the height limits and the outriggers, and they must be on site and followed. The steps below show the usual pattern only.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Read the maker's instructions and the access plan
Check every component, and tag and set aside any faulty part
Check the ground and look up for overhead hazards
Set up the exclusion zone with barriers and signs
Brief the team: roles, signals, PPE (hard hat, safety boots, gloves, and a harness where the rules require one)
Fit the castors to the base frames and lock every brake
Join the base frames with the horizontal and diagonal braces in the order the maker shows
Level the base using the adjustable legs, and check it with a spirit level
Fit the outriggers as the instructions require for the height and the place (indoors or outdoors)
Build up frame by frame, fitting the braces as you go
Fit each platform, and fit the guardrails for the next level from the protected level below, by the through-the-trapdoor method or the maker's advance guardrail system
Fit toe boards at the working platform
Check the height is within the limit for the base and outriggers
A competent person inspects the tower and completes the tag before anyone uses it

blocks.p: In the **through-the-trapdoor method**, the erector climbs the built-in ladder and sits in the trapdoor of the platform, with the body still below platform level, while fitting the guardrails for that level. Only when the guardrails are in place does the erector stand up on the platform.

The maker gives the greatest platform height for each base size, with and without outriggers, and usually a lower limit outdoors than indoors because of wind. Many instructions express it as a ratio of height to the **shortest side of the base**. Example: if the limit without outriggers is 3 to 1 and the base is 1.35 m by 2.5 m, the platform may be no higher than 3 × 1.35 = 4.05 m. For a higher platform, fit the outriggers the instructions specify.

flow: Lay sole boards where needed and place base plates or base jacks on them
Stand the first frames, fit the braces, and level and square the first lift with a spirit level and tape before going higher: any error at the base gets worse with every lift
Fit the boards of the first working level, fully boarded and supported
Fit guardrails, mid rails and toe boards at each working level before anyone works there
Build up lift by lift, bracing as you go and fitting ties where the plan shows, as the scaffold reaches them
Set up the access ladder: tied, at an angle of about 1 out for every 4 up (about 75°), extending about 1 m above the landing
Inspect, tag, and hand over for use

ul: Agree simple words or signals before passing parts up and down, such as "taking" and "got it", so each person knows when to take hold and when to let go.
Pass parts by hand from person to person, or raise them on a rope; never throw them.
Keep three points of contact on ladders and frames; carry tools and parts up on a line, not in your hands.
Never climb the outside of the frames or the braces; use the built-in ladder or stairs.
**Fully boarded**, with no wide gaps that someone could trip on or drop tools through.
Boards **supported** at the spacing the standard or maker gives (often about 1.2 m for common timber scaffold boards), resting squarely on their supports and secured so they cannot slide or lift.

Board ends overhang their last support by only a small amount, as the standard says (often between about 50 and 150 mm): too little and the board can slip off; too much and it can tip up when stepped on.
The platform is wide enough for the work, the welder and the tools, and kept clear of offcuts and slag.

blocks.p: Every open side of a platform from which a person could fall has a **top guardrail** (about 1 m high; many standards ask for between about 950 mm and 1.1 m), a **mid rail** roughly halfway, and a **toe board** at least about 150 mm high. Follow the standard the Centre uses and the maker's instructions.

ul: Guardrails are fitted before anyone works on that level, and stay in place until that level is taken down.
Nobody sits on, stands on or leans over a guardrail, or stands on boxes, drums or buckets on the platform to gain height.
A **full-body harness** with a lanyard is worn where guardrails are not yet in place and the Centre's rules or the plan require it.
The lanyard is clipped to a strong anchor point that the plan approves, never to a toe board, a guardrail clip or a loose part.

Check the harness before each use: webbing, stitching, buckles, the lanyard and its connectors. A lanyard whose **energy absorber** has started to tear open, or a harness that has held a fall, is withdrawn from use and not used again.
Wear it fitted snugly, as the maker shows.

blocks.p: A person left hanging in a harness is in danger even if uninjured: the leg straps restrict the blood flow and they can faint within minutes (**suspension trauma**). Every job where harnesses are used needs a rescue plan that can bring the person down quickly, using equipment and trained people already on site, not just a phone number.

blocks.note: Calling 110 for fire and ambulance is part of the plan, but the emergency services may take too long to reach a person hanging in a harness. The plan must say who will rescue the person, how, and with what equipment.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Before it is used for the first time.
After any alteration, by anyone, however small: an extra lift, a moved board, a removed brace.
After anything that could have affected it: strong wind, heavy rain, an impact by a vehicle or load, work nearby that disturbed the ground.
At regular intervals, as the Centre's rules set (often every 7 days).

blocks.p: Inspections are done by a **competent person**: someone trained and experienced enough to spot faults and judge whether the scaffold is safe.

head: Area
Checks
rows: Base
Ground not sunk or washed out; sole boards, base plates and jacks in place; jacks within their limit; castor brakes locked
Structure
Standards plumb; ledgers and transoms in place; braces complete; couplers and clips tight; nothing removed
Ties and stability
Ties in place and sound; outriggers fitted as required; height within the limit
Platform
Fully boarded, boards sound and secure, no trip hazards, not overloaded
Edge protection
Guardrails, mid rails and toe boards on every open side
Access
Ladder or stairs sound, tied, extending above the landing
Suitability
Still right for the job and the loads

blocks.p: The result is written in the **inspection register**, with the date and the inspector's name.

ul: A **tag** is fixed at every access point. One side or colour shows the scaffold has been inspected and is safe to use, with the date and the inspector's signature; another shows it must **not** be used.
Users look at the tag **every time** before they climb.
No tag, an unsafe tag, or an inspection date that is out of date means: do not use it, keep others off it, and report it to the supervisor.
Only the competent person changes a tag. Nobody else writes a new date on it.

blocks.note: A scaffold inspected on Monday is not safe on Wednesday if someone has altered it on Tuesday. Any alteration needs a new inspection before use.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Welding from a scaffold, and site hazards

head: Precaution
Why
rows: Hot-work permit where the Centre or site uses one
Makes sure the fire precautions are checked and signed before work starts
Platform cleared; fire blankets over timber boards and around the work
Timber boards, rubbish and nearby materials can catch fire from spatter and slag
Fire watch with a suitable extinguisher, during the work and for the set time after it
Smouldering material can flare up long after welding stops
Area below cleared and barricaded
Sparks and slag fall a long way and burn people and materials below
Welding return lead clamped to the work, close to the weld, never to the scaffold
Current through tubes and couplers can overheat them, damage them and give shocks
Leads raised on a line and tied along a route clear of the ladder and trapdoor
Loose leads trip people and snag on parts; leads carried up by hand break the three points of contact
Gas cylinders upright and secured on the ground, clear of the work; only the hoses go up
A cylinder on a platform can fall, be hit by sparks, or overload it
No welding or cutting on any scaffold part
Heat weakens tubes, frames and couplers that carry the load
Scaffold checked for heat damage after the hot work
Arc strikes and heat can leave hidden damage

blocks.note: Aluminium towers lose strength at temperatures far below those of welding, and an arc strike can damage a tube. Keep the arc, spatter and hot slag off the frames, and screen the tower from the work if needed.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Scaffold tubes and towers conduct electricity. If a scaffold or tower must go near overhead power lines, stop and get advice from the power company and the Centre before anything is put up. Never carry long tubes upright near lines.

blocks.h: Site and weather hazards in Jamaica

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Heavy rain and soft or washed-out ground
Sole boards and base plates; re-inspect the base after rain
Strong wind, tropical storms and hurricanes (season 1 June to 30 November)
Follow the maker's wind limits; stop work when they are reached
No sheeting or tarpaulins without design advice
Tie down or dismantle towers and loose parts before a storm
Sea air
Inspect steel parts for corrosion; store parts dry
Hot sun
Metal frames get hot to touch: gloves, water and breaks
Vehicles and forklifts
Barricades, signs and a marked route clear of the scaffold
The public, guests and customers
Exclusion zone, covered walkway or diverted path; never work over people

blocks.p: Many tower makers tell users to stop work on the tower when the wind reaches about Force 4 on the Beaufort scale (around 27 km/h) and to tie the tower in or take it down if winds above about Force 6 (around 40–50 km/h) are expected. Use the figures in your tower's instructions.

sections.title: Dismantling, storage and leading the team

flow: Check that the work is finished and that all tools and materials are off the platforms
Tag the scaffold "not to be used" and set up the exclusion zone with barriers and signs
Follow the maker's instructions or the method: usually the reverse of erection, working from the top down
Keep the guardrails at each level in place until that level itself is being taken down; harnesses where the rules require
Pass parts down by hand, person to person, or lower them on a rope; never throw or drop them
Remove each tie only when the scaffold has come down to it, so the rest stays stable
At ground level, sort, clean and check the parts; tag and set aside any that are damaged
Clean up the area and remove the barriers last

blocks.note: If dismantling cannot be finished in one day, leave what remains stable and braced, with its ties and guardrails, tag it "not to be used", remove or block the access ladder, and keep the barriers up overnight.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Sort parts by type and size, and store them on racks off the ground, under cover where possible.
Clean couplers and oil their threads as the maker says.
Keep damaged parts apart, tagged, for repair by a competent person or scrapping.
Store tower components with their instruction manual, and count them so missing parts are noticed before the next job.

flow: Brief the team at the job with the scaffold instructor: the task, the type of tower or scaffold, the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules on who may erect it
Go over the hazards and controls: exclusion zone, PPE, harnesses, no climbing on frames, passing parts by hand
Give each person a clear role, such as checking parts, passing, assembling and signalling, and agree the signals
Supervise each step against the instructions; check the base is level and the brakes are on
Stop the work at once if anything is unsafe
Make sure nobody uses the scaffold until it is inspected and tagged
Afterwards, record the inspection, report faulty parts, and ask the team what went well and what to improve

blocks.note: If someone in your team starts to climb a tower or scaffold with no tag, an unsafe tag or an out-of-date tag, stop them. Being the team leader means stopping unsafe work even when it is only "for a minute".
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain the Centre's rules on who may erect, alter and dismantle scaffolds.
I can compare a ladder, a mobile tower, a frame scaffold and a MEWP, and choose the best access for a welding job.
I can survey a site and write an access plan.
I can name the parts of a scaffold and the couplers, and say what each one does.
I can prepare a firm, level base, using sole boards, base plates and base jacks correctly.
I can explain why ties need sound anchorage and why sheeting is not added without advice.
I can explain platform loads and why point loads are dangerous.
I can check components and deal with faulty ones.
I can describe how a trained team erects a mobile tower and a frame scaffold, following the maker's instructions.
I can work out a tower's height limit from its base and the maker's ratio.
I can set up a ladder correctly for access.
I can describe full edge protection and a fully boarded platform.
I can check and use a harness, and explain why a rescue plan is needed.
I can explain when scaffolds are inspected, what is checked, and how tags are used.
I can list the precautions for welding and cutting from a scaffold, and explain each one.
I can name the weather and site hazards for scaffolds in Jamaica and their controls.
I can describe safe dismantling and storage.
I can brief, organise and supervise a team putting up a tower.

terms: An adjustable screw base used to level a scaffold on uneven ground
A steel plate under a standard that spreads its load
The space between two pairs of standards along a scaffold
A diagonal tube that stops a scaffold swaying
The lock on a tower wheel, set before anyone climbs
Someone with the training and experience to inspect and judge a scaffold
The part of a lanyard that tears open to soften the jolt of a fall
A barricaded area people must not enter while a scaffold is erected or dismantled
A person who watches for fire during hot work and for a set time after it
A rail along an open platform edge to stop people falling
Full-body equipment connected by a lanyard to an anchor, to stop a fall
A horizontal tube along the length of a scaffold, joining the standards
The height from one level of ledgers to the next
Mobile elevating work platform, such as a scissor lift or boom lift
An arm that widens a tower's base to make it more stable
A coupler that holds a transom onto a ledger; not load-bearing for ledgers
A fitting that joins two tubes end to end
A timber board under base plates that spreads the load on soft ground
Fainting and worse caused by hanging still in a harness
A coupler that joins two tubes at any angle
The label at a scaffold's access point that shows whether it may be used
Fitting the guardrails of a new level while sitting in the platform's trapdoor
A fixing that holds a scaffold to a structure
An upright board along a platform edge that stops things being kicked off
A short tube across the scaffold's width that carries the boards

c1.title: Brackets on a tank in Port Royal
c1.text: Okeil Morris leads a team welding new brackets to the outside of a steel water tank at a marine workshop in Port Royal, Kingston. They will work from a mobile aluminium tower with a base of 1.35 m by 2.5 m. The maker's instructions say that, without outriggers, the platform may be no higher than 3 times the shortest side of the base; the job needs a platform at 4.5 m. The tower stands on a level concrete slab beside the harbour, where strong sea breezes blow most afternoons. A welder wants to tie a tarpaulin across one side of the tower for shade, and another plans to carry the welding lead up the ladder over his shoulder.

c2.title: A frame scaffold at a church in Junction
c2.text: Javaun Grant is leading a trained crew putting up a two-lift frame scaffold against the wall of an old church in Junction, St Elizabeth, so that a steel canopy can be welded on. The ground slopes, and one base plate would land on a cast-iron drain cover. On the low side, a crew member has wound one base jack out almost to the end of its thread. During the component check a trainee finds a timber board with a long split and a missing end band. The church wall is old stone with loose mortar in places, and the plan shows two ties into it.

c3.title: A hotel balcony in Runaway Bay
c3.text: Sherika Allen's team is building a tube-and-fitting scaffold to weld a new steel balcony frame on a hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, beside the public footpath to the beach. A trainee has run out of right-angle couplers and has fixed a ledger to a standard with a putlog coupler. The welders plan to stack twelve lengths of steel in one pile in the middle of a platform bay. The scaffold was inspected and tagged on Monday; on Wednesday the hotel's maintenance men added a short extra lift to reach a gutter.

c4.title: A training tower in Harbour View
c4.text: Rohan Edwards leads a group of trainees putting up an aluminium tower in a warehouse in Harbour View, Kingston, under the Centre's scaffold instructor, using the through-the-trapdoor method. The Centre's rules require harnesses during erection. While checking the harnesses, a trainee finds that the energy absorber on one lanyard has partly torn open. The group's rescue plan says only "call 110". On a second tower nearby, the tag at the access point is signed and dated nine days ago; the Centre's rules call for an inspection every seven days.

c5.title: Taking down a scaffold in Moneague
c5.text: Mr Desmond Palmer is supervising a trained crew taking down a three-lift frame scaffold, tied to the wall of a factory in Moneague, St Ann. To save time, one crew member suggests taking out all the wall ties first. By 5 p.m. the scaffold is only half dismantled, and the crew will finish the next morning.

questions.q: Can Okeil's team set the platform at 4.5 m without outriggers?
o: Yes, as long as all four castor brakes are locked
Yes, because the concrete slab is firm and level
Yes: the limit is 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 m, so 4.5 m is fine
No: 3 × 1.35 m allows only 4.05 m
questions.why: The ratio is applied to the shortest side of the base: 3 × 1.35 m = 4.05 m. A 4.5 m platform needs the outriggers the instructions specify, and outdoors in a sea breeze the limits matter even more.

questions.q: Why must the welders keep the arc, spatter and hot slag off the tower's tubes?
o: Spatter would stick to the tubes and spoil their finish
Hot tubes would make the castor brakes slip on the slab
Spatter on the tubes would hide the inspection tag
Heat and arc strikes weaken aluminium tubes
questions.why: Aluminium loses strength at temperatures far below welding heat, and an arc strike can damage a tube. The frames carry the load, so they are screened from the work and checked afterwards.

questions.q: Why should the tarpaulin not be tied across the tower?
o: It would act as a sail and topple the tower
Its weight would overload the tower's platform
The sun would rot it within a few days
It would make the tower too heavy to push along
questions.why: Sheeting greatly increases the wind load on a tower or scaffold, and sea breezes at Port Royal are strong. Sheeting is fitted only when the design or the maker's instructions allow for it, with the extra ties or ballast they require.

questions.q: How should the welding lead get up to the platform?
o: Carried up over the welder's shoulder as he climbs
Raised on a line, then tied clear of the ladder
Draped loose over the guardrail so it slides as he moves
Laid across the trapdoor where it is easy to reach
questions.why: Climbing needs three points of contact, so nothing heavy is carried up by hand. A lead tied along a planned route cannot trip anyone, snag on parts or block the way up.

questions.q: What should Javaun do about the leg that would land on the drain cover?
o: Stand it on the cover, as cast iron is very strong
Put a brick under the base plate to lift it off the cover
Move the leg, or bridge the cover as approved
Lift the cover out so the leg rests on the drain floor
questions.why: A drain cover can crack or tip under a point load, and a brick can split or slide. The leg is moved, or the cover is bridged with timbers or a beam that a competent person approves.

questions.q: What should be done about the base jack wound out almost to the end of its thread?
o: Leave it, as levelling is exactly what a base jack is for
Keep it in its limit; level the low side another way
Pack under its base plate with loose bricks or offcuts
Tilt the frames slightly so the jack can be shortened
questions.why: A jack wound out too far is weak and can bend or pull out of the standard. The low side is built up in a way the maker or a competent person approves, such as stepped sole boards or a different frame height.

questions.q: What should happen to the split board with no end band?
o: Use it at the end of the platform, where loads are lighter
Nail a batten across the split and use it as normal
Turn it upside down so the split is underneath
Tag it as faulty, set it apart and report it
questions.why: A split board can snap under a person, and the end band stops splits spreading. Faulty parts are tagged and quarantined so nobody uses them by mistake, then repaired by a competent person or scrapped.

questions.q: What should be done about the ties into the old stone wall?
o: Fix them as planned, since the plan shows two ties
Have the anchors tested, or use rakers instead
Leave them out, as a two-lift scaffold needs no ties
Tie the scaffold to the church's drainpipe instead
questions.why: A tie is only as good as its anchor, and loose stonework may not hold. A competent person tests the anchors, or the scaffold is held with rakers or buttresses instead. Drainpipes and gutters are never anchors.

questions.q: Why is the putlog coupler wrong for joining the ledger to the standard?
o: Nothing is wrong, as every coupler has the same strength
It is made to hold transoms, not ledgers
It is fine if the bolt is tightened extra hard
It is fine on the lower lifts, where it carries less
questions.why: A ledger-to-standard joint carries the platform's load down to the standard and needs a load-bearing right-angle coupler. A putlog coupler can slip under that load. The trainee must wait for the right fitting.

questions.q: How should the steel for the balcony be placed on the platform?
o: Spread in small stacks near the standards
In one pile, as long as the total is within the rating
Leaning against the guardrail to keep the boards clear
On the top lift, where it is out of everyone's way
questions.why: Twelve lengths in one pile make a point load that can break a board even when the total is within the rating. Small stacks near the standards and transoms spread the load, and guardrails are never used to hold materials.

questions.q: The scaffold is beside a public footpath. How should the public be protected while the team welds?
o: Put up a sign asking people to walk past quickly
Weld only at moments when nobody is walking by
Leave the path open, as the work is above head height
Divert the path, or give it a covered walkway
questions.why: Sparks, slag and dropped tools fall onto anyone below, and passers-by cannot be relied on to read signs. The path is closed and diverted, or protected with a covered walkway and barriers, as the plan says.

questions.q: Can Sherika's team use the scaffold on Thursday?
o: Yes, as it passed its inspection on Monday
Yes, but only on the lifts the maintenance men did not touch
Not until a competent person re-inspects and re-tags it
Yes, once the maintenance men have signed the tag
questions.why: Any alteration, by anyone, means the scaffold must be inspected again before use. The added lift may have changed the loads, the bracing or the ties, and the Monday tag no longer describes the scaffold.

questions.q: Using the through-the-trapdoor method, where is the trainee while fitting the guardrails of a new platform?
o: Standing on the new platform, holding on to a frame
Standing on the top rail of the level below
Sitting in the trapdoor, still below the platform
Outside the tower, on the rungs of the end frame
questions.why: Sitting in the trapdoor keeps the body below the new platform, protected by the level below, while the guardrails go on. Only then does the trainee stand up on the platform.

questions.q: What should happen to the lanyard with the partly torn energy absorber?
o: Use it, as the webbing itself is still in one piece
Tape the absorber closed and use it for today
Withdraw it, as it may have held a fall
Use it, but clip it to a lower anchor point
questions.why: The absorber tears open to soften the jolt of a fall, so a torn one may have done its job once and cannot be trusted again. It is withdrawn from use, reported and replaced.

questions.q: What is wrong with a rescue plan that says only "call 110"?
o: A person hanging in a harness must be freed fast
Nothing, as the fire brigade carries out all rescues
It should say to call the harness supplier first
It should say to cut the lanyard to lower the person
questions.why: Hanging still in a harness can cause fainting within minutes (suspension trauma). The plan must name who will rescue the person, how, and with what equipment already on site; calling 110 is only part of it.

questions.q: What should the group do about the second tower's tag?
o: Keep off it, as its inspection has lapsed
Use it, as the tag is signed and still in place
Use it, as two days over the limit hardly matters
Check it themselves and write today's date on the tag
questions.why: A tag is only valid for the period the rules set. At nine days old the inspection has lapsed, so nobody uses the tower until a competent person inspects it. Only the inspector changes the tag.

questions.q: What is wrong with taking out all the wall ties first?
o: Nothing: ties are only needed while the scaffold is used
The ties should be left in the wall for the next job
The scaffold could pull away or topple before it is down
It is fine as long as the guardrails stay in place
questions.why: The ties keep the scaffold stable all the way down. Each tie is removed only when dismantling has reached its level, as the method says.

questions.q: What should be done at 5 p.m. with the half-dismantled scaffold?
o: Leave it as it is, since the crew will be back early
Leave the ladder up so the crew can start quickly
Take out the lowest braces so nobody can climb it
Leave it stable, tagged unusable, ladder removed
questions.why: A partly dismantled scaffold must be left stable, with the ties and guardrails that remain, tagged "not to be used", with the ladder removed or blocked and the barriers up. Removing braces would make it unstable.

questions.q: Twelve brackets are to be welded 6 m up, spread along a 30 m wall of a warehouse with a firm, level concrete floor. A scissor lift and a trained operator are available for the two days. Which access suits the job best?
o: A ladder, moved along to each bracket in turn
The scissor lift, with its trained operator
A mobile tower, pushed along with the welder on top
A pallet on forklift forks, raised to each bracket
questions.why: Welding needs both hands and a guarded platform, so a ladder is not suitable. A MEWP suits short tasks spread along a wall on firm, level ground. A tower must never be moved with anyone on it, and people never ride on forks.

questions.q: In a yard by the sea, some steel scaffold tubes show heavy rust and pitting at their ends. What should be done with them?
o: Set them apart for a competent person to judge
Paint them so they look new and use them as normal
Use them only for guardrails and toe-board supports
Cut the rusty ends off and weld on new pieces
questions.why: Pitting thins the tube wall and weakens it, often worst at the ends and inside. A competent person decides whether the tubes are fit to use; scaffold parts are never repaired by welding.
